query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Variations in stacking fault energy (SFE) induced by changes in elemental interactions govern the mechanical behavior differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets. In particular, removing one or more elements alters the local chemical environment and lattice distortions, which in turn shifts the SFE to modify dislocation mobility and twinning activation during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni single‐phase FCC alloy produced by standardized thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Prepare compositionally reduced (quaternary and ternary) alloys by selectively omitting one or two elements while keeping equal atomic fractions among remaining species; process all samples using identical thermomechanical conditions.
generation.conditions: Test under identical deformation conditions (e.g., strain rate, temperature, and loading protocols) ensuring all alloys remain single-phase FCC.
generation.structural_mediator: Altered local chemical environments leading to systematic changes in stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: Changing the constituent count adjusts local lattice distortions and short-range chemical interactions, which modify the stacking fault energy. These changes affect the balance between dislocation glide and deformation twinning, thus governing yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, specific quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit measurable shifts in SFE that correlate with altered dislocation behavior: for example, a higher SFE may reduce twinning and enhance yield strength, while a lower SFE may increase twinning and ductility. The direction of these changes is predictable based on the known effects of each element on the SFE.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, with established SFE values and corresponding mechanical properties measured under controlled conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in FCC single-phase high-entropy alloys produced under similar thermomechanical histories; it may not apply when secondary phases form or when processing-induced microstructural differences dominate behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the SFE changes and the extent to which these changes alone explain mechanical property differences remain uncertain due to possible competing effects (e.g., conventional solution strengthening or processing-related defects).

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the equiatomic quinary alloy and a systematic series of quaternary and ternary variants. Characterize the SFE of each alloy using transmission electron microscopy (observing partial dislocation separation and twin formation) and/or indirect techniques such as measuring critical resolved shear stresses. Perform standardized mechanical tests (e.g., tension/compression testing) to evaluate yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Direct or indirect SFE measurements (e.g., via TEM analysis of dislocation cores and twin nucleation)
Yield strength, ductility, and stress–strain responses under identical deformation conditions
Microstructural analysis to confirm single-phase FCC structure and deformation mechanisms
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured SFEs do not show systematic shifts correlating with changes in elemental composition, or if the observed mechanical property changes (yield strength, ductility, twinning activity) do not correlate with the predicted SFE variations relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
